title: A New Heaven and a New Earth
lead: History does not end in suffering, death, or decay. God makes all things new.
questions: Whom will I tell this week, as simply as I can, the one sentence that has carried us through these forty days: there is hope?
What am I still trying to buy from God or earn from Him, even though the Bible’s final offer is: freely?
Which sentence from these forty days am I taking with me for good, and in what situation in my life should it start to work?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Forty days ago we stood in Eden and heard the promise of an offspring who would crush the serpent’s head. Today we open the last pages of the Bible and discover that Scripture ends in a garden: the last chapters of Revelation answer the first chapters of Genesis point by point. “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth.” The Greek kainos means new in quality, not simply the next one. God does not throw His creation away like a failed project; He renews it. And the promise comes with a signature: “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.”

“And the sea was no more”: the Greek text has the definite article, so it means that sea. John writes as an old man exiled on Patmos, cut off by water from everyone he loved. In the new world there will be nothing left that separates and threatens. And the heart of the vision beats in one sentence: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.” Notice the direction: people are not evacuated upward; the city comes “down out of heaven.” The Bible’s finale is God moving in with us. And His first act after the move: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” Personally, like a mother with her child. The city has a shape that was an easily read code: its length, width, and height are equal. The only cube in the Bible was the Most Holy Place, which one man entered once a year. The Bible ends with the Most Holy Place stretched out over an entire city; that is why there is no temple there, because all of it is temple.

The river and the tree of life from Eden return too, and “the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations”: in a world without disease, the last wound to be healed is the division between people. And the greatest promise of all: “They will see His face,” the very thing Moses was refused. “No longer will there be any curse.” This is not a reward for merit. It is the return of what was stolen.

This is why we walked for forty days: to learn one sentence in forty scenes. There is hope. And a hope like this cannot be kept under a basket; all around us are people in their own storms and beside their own empty nets. They don’t need a lecture. They need someone who will sit down by their well and say: there is hope, and I know Hope by name.

Forty days ago we stood in Eden. We watched trust in God crack, watched a man hide among the trees, watched the garden gate close behind the first human beings. And we heard a promise: the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head. Today, on the last day of our journey, we open the final pages of the Bible and discover something planned from the very start: Scripture ends in a garden. The last two chapters of Revelation answer the first three chapters of Genesis point by point, as if someone were closing a bracket around the whole history of the world. This is no accidental symmetry. It is the same story, carried through to its end.

sections.heading: I Make All Things New
paragraphs: John writes: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth.” The word “new” is worth pausing over, because Greek has two words for newness. One means new in the sense of “next, different, starting from scratch.” John uses the other: kainos, new in quality. The new earth is not a replacement planet; it is this same earth, cleansed and restored to the shape it was meant to have. For anyone who loves this world, the difference is enormous: God does not throw His creation away like a failed project. He renews it. “Behold, I make all things new,” says the One seated on the throne, and it is one of the few sentences in Revelation that God speaks in person. And right after it comes a second, which reads like a signature at the bottom of a document: “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.” The hope with which we close this series is not a mood or a streak of optimism. It is a written promise, signed.

sections.heading: The Sea Is No More
paragraphs: The very first sentence of this vision contains a strange detail: “and the sea was no more.” Why, of all things, should the sea disappear from a perfect world? The Greek text has the definite article here: that sea is no more, a particular one. John writes these words as an old man exiled on Patmos, a rocky island from which he looked out every day at the water separating him from everyone he loved and from all the churches he was responsible for. To him the sea was not a vacation view; it was a wall of water. And in the Bible, from the very beginning, the sea is a picture of chaos and threat, the element that had to be rebuked for the world to come into being, and that nearly swallowed the boat on the lake on the thirty-third day of our journey. So the sentence “the sea was no more” means: nothing is left that separates, and nothing is left that threatens. In the new world there will be no water between you and the people you love.

sections.heading: The Dwelling Place of God Is with Man
paragraphs: And then comes the sentence that is the heart of the whole vision, and really the heart of the whole Bible: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.” Let’s trace that arc, because it has run through our entire series. In the wilderness God had a tent built for Himself so He could live in the middle of the camp. Then, as we read on day twenty-eight, “The Word became flesh”: God pitched His tent in human skin. And here, at the end, His presence stops being a tent, a temple, or a visit. It becomes a permanent address. And notice the direction, because it overturns the most popular picture of heaven: people are not taken up; the city comes “down out of heaven from God.” The Bible’s finale is not an evacuation of people from the earth but God moving in with people. The same God who asked in Eden, “Where are you?”, who came down to Bethel on the stairway of Jacob’s dream, who took on flesh in Bethlehem, takes the final step: He moves in with us for good. And the first thing He does after the move is not a lecture or a judgment but the tenderest gesture in all of Scripture: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” Not “tears will disappear.” He will wipe them away, personally, the way a mother does for her child. Only then comes the list of what will be no more: death, mourning, crying, and pain. Everything we have walked through in this series, the whole catalog of human misery from the flood to the sieges, gets its expiration date here.

sections.heading: A City That Is the Most Holy Place
paragraphs: John describes the New Jerusalem in detail and gives measurements that anyone who knew the Old Testament would have decoded at once: the city’s length, width, and height are equal. A cube. In the entire Bible up to that point there had been only one room with those proportions: the Most Holy Place of the temple, the space behind the curtain that one man entered once a year. The Bible ends with the Most Holy Place stretched out over the whole city of God. That is why John points out that he saw no temple in that city: not because it is missing, but because all of it is temple. The building was only ever a promise of an address. The privilege that for centuries belonged to one high priest for a few minutes a year will be the everyday life of all the redeemed. We remember the curtain torn at the moment of Jesus’ death, four days ago on our journey; here we see where that tearing was leading. God tore curtains so that in the end there would be none left at all.

sections.heading: The River and the Tree
paragraphs: In the Bible’s last chapter, exactly the two things that stood at the center of Eden return: a river and the tree of life. The river flows from the throne, and the tree yields fresh fruit every month. But one detail is new: “the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” In a world without disease or death, leaves cannot be healing bodies; the Greek speaks explicitly of healing nations, not individuals. The last wound God binds up in the Bible is the division between people: national, tribal, racial, linguistic, all the walls humanity has been building since Babel. Our series began with broken trust between human beings and God; it ends with the healing of what has broken between human beings too. And one more promise, the greatest: “They will see His face.” That was refused even to Moses, who asked, “Please show me Your glory,” and was told that no one can see God’s face and live. Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, whose name means “face of God,” waited for decades to see God’s face in the face of an infant. Here the waiting of every generation comes to an end: they will see His face, unveiled, without fear, forever. And over it all stands a short sentence from Revelation: “No longer will there be any curse.” The curse of Genesis 3, the thorns, the sweat, the pain, and death, is revoked. This is not a reward for our merits. It is the return of what was stolen.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: So ends our forty-day journey together, and it is fair to ask why we made it. Not so we would know more about Noah, Ruth, or Peter. We walked so that we could learn one sentence in forty scenes: there is hope. When everything has fallen apart and when you are at the end of your strength. When you feel like a stranger, a failure, overlooked, stuck. When the boat is sinking, the bread has run out, and the tomb is closing. When the end looks final. In every one of these situations we met the same God: one who comes out to meet people, comes down to where they are, asks, listens, feeds, weeps, calls people by name, and writes the next chapter after the words “The End.” Today’s reading tells us where He is taking all of it: to a home where He will live with us for good. Christian hope is not a fortune-teller’s promise that everything will turn out fine. It is the written promise of the One who calls Himself the Alpha and the Omega, and who said: “To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life.” Freely. The Bible’s final offer costs nothing, like everything that mattered most in this series. And if these forty days have taught us anything as a community, let them teach us one more thing: a hope like this cannot be kept under a basket. All around us live people who are today exactly where the characters in these stories were: in their own storm, beside their own empty nets, on the road to their own Emmaus. They don’t need a lecture from us. They need someone who will sit down by their well and say: there is hope. I know Hope by name.
